from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "A distribution shows how data spreads out.",
            "Uniform distributions mean all outcomes are equally likely.",
            "Rolling a die creates a uniform distribution."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: The Concept of Distribution", lecture_lines)
        
        # Animation Elements
        dot = Dot(color=WHITE)
        points = VGroup(*[Dot(point=np.random.normal(0, 0.5, 3), color="#FF00FF") for _ in range(50)])
        box = Rectangle(color="#00FFFF", width=2, height=2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.place_at_grid(dot, 'C3')
        self.play(FadeIn(dot))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FF00FF"))
        self.place_at_grid(points, 'C4')
        self.play(FadeIn(points))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00FFFF"))
        self.place_in_area(box, 'B2', 'E5')
        self.play(Create(box))
        
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Hook: The Chaos of One vs. The Order of Many", 
                          ["What happens when we average multiple samples?", 
                           "One sample is random and chaotic.", 
                           "Many samples averaged become predictable."])
        
        # Define elements
        particle = Dot(color="#FF4500", radius=0.1)
        particles = VGroup(*[Dot(color="#FF4500", radius=0.05) for _ in range(100)])
        wave = FunctionGraph(lambda x: 0.5 * np.sin(3 * x), x_range=[-1.5, 1.5], color="#00FF00")
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Color line
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FF4500"))
        # Animation: Start with a single chaotic particle
        self.place_at_grid(particle, 'C3')
        self.play(FadeIn(particle))
        self.play(particle.animate.shift(UP * 0.5), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(particle.animate.shift(LEFT * 0.5), run_time=0.5)
        self.play(particle.animate.shift(DOWN * 0.8), run_time=0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Color line
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#FF4500"))
        # Animation: Populate screen
        for p in particles:
            self.place_in_area(p, 'B4', 'E6')
        self.play(LaggedStart(*[FadeIn(p) for p in particles], lag_ratio=0.01))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Color line
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        # Animation: Smooth movement
        self.place_in_area(wave, 'B4', 'E6')
        self.play(FadeOut(particles), FadeIn(wave))
        self.play(wave.animate.set_stroke(width=4), run_time=2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "The CLT explains this magic.",
            "Sample means approach a normal distribution.",
            "This happens regardless of population shape.",
            "Increase sample size for better approximation.",
            "The bell curve always emerges."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Core Concept: The Normal Approximation", lecture_lines)

        # Initial bar chart setup
        axes = Axes(x_range=[-4, 4, 1], y_range=[0, 1, 0.2], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        chart = VGroup(*[Rectangle(height=0.1, width=0.5, color="#1E90FF", fill_opacity=1) for _ in range(5)])
        chart.arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1)
        self.place_at_grid(chart, 'C3')

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#1E90FF")
        self.play(FadeIn(chart))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#1E90FF")
        new_chart = VGroup(*[Rectangle(height=np.random.rand()*1.5, width=0.2, color="#1E90FF", fill_opacity=1) for _ in range(20)])
        new_chart.arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.05)
        self.place_at_grid(new_chart, 'D3')
        self.play(Transform(chart, new_chart))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FFFF00")
        curve = FunctionGraph(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2), x_range=[-3, 3], color="#FFFF00")
        self.place_at_grid(curve, 'C3', scale_factor=0.8)
        self.play(Create(curve))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.play(FadeOut(chart))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#FF0000")
        peak = Dot(color="#FF0000").move_to(curve.point_from_proportion(0.5))
        self.play(Indicate(peak))
        self.wait(1)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Visualizing the Bell Curve", [
            "Two key parameters emerge: mean and variance.", 
            "The mean of means equals population mean.", 
            "Variance shrinks as sample size grows."
        ])
        
        # Bell curve elements
        axes = Axes(x_range=[-4, 4, 1], y_range=[0, 1, 0.2], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        bell_curve = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2 / 2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi), color=WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(axes, "A1", "F6", scale_factor=0.6)
        axes.add(bell_curve)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(Create(bell_curve), run_time=2)
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#87CEEB"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        mean_line = Line(axes.c2p(0, 0), axes.c2p(0, 0.4), color="#00FF00")
        self.play(Create(mean_line))
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        left_sd = axes.c2p(-1, 0)
        right_sd = axes.c2p(1, 0)
        # Create shaded region
        shaded_area = axes.get_area(bell_curve, x_range=[-1, 1], color="#FFD700", opacity=0.3)
        self.play(FadeIn(shaded_area))
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFD700"))
        
        self.wait(2)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Application: Real-World Predictability", [
            "CLT allows population inference from samples.",
            "We predict outcomes without knowing original shapes.",
            "It bridges sample data to real-world certainty."
        ])

        # Create histogram data
        data = np.random.normal(0, 1, 1000)
        axes = Axes(x_range=[-3, 3, 1], y_range=[0, 0.5, 0.1], axis_config={"include_tip": False})
        hist = BarChart(values=np.histogram(data, bins=20, range=(-3, 3))[0], bar_names=[str(i) for i in range(20)])
        hist_group = self.place_in_area(hist, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=0.7)

        # Create Normal Curve
        curve = FunctionGraph(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2 / 2) / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi), x_range=[-3, 3])
        curve.set_color(WHITE)
        self.place_in_area(curve, "B2", "E5", scale_factor=0.7)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(hist_group))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#ADFF2F")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(Create(curve))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(Indicate(curve, color="#FF0000", scale_factor=1.2))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FF0000")
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Central Limit Theorem (CLT): The Magic of Averages

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Distribution
sections.content: Briefly review that a distribution is a way of showing how data is spread out. Introduce the 'Uniform Distribution' (where all outcomes are equally likely) as our starting point.
sections.example: Imagine a fair 6-sided die. Rolling it once gives a flat, uniform distribution of outcomes (1 through 6).

sections.title: The Hook: The Chaos of One vs. The Order of Many
sections.content: Pose the question: What happens if we take multiple samples and calculate their average? Visually contrast a single sample's distribution with the distribution of the 'mean of samples'.
sections.example: If you roll one die, the result is random. If you roll 50 dice and take their average, the result will almost always be close to 3.5. Why does the chaos vanish?

sections.title: Core Concept: The Normal Approximation
sections.content: Define the CLT: As the sample size (n) increases, the distribution of sample means approaches a Normal Distribution (Bell Curve), regardless of the shape of the original population distribution.
sections.example: Visual animation: Start with a wildly skewed 'Exponential' distribution. As we increase the number of items being averaged (n=2, n=5, n=30), the graph morphs in real-time into a smooth, symmetrical bell curve.

sections.title: Visualizing the Bell Curve
sections.content: Highlight the two key parameters that emerge from the CLT: the mean of the sample means (which equals the population mean) and the shrinking variance (standard error).
sections.example: Show a 'Galton Board' animation where thousands of marbles bounce through pegs; even though each marble's path is random, they pile up to form a perfect bell curve.

sections.title: Application: Real-World Predictability
sections.content: Explain why this is powerful: The CLT allows us to make predictions about populations even when we don't know the original distribution shape. It is the bridge between sample data and population inference.
sections.example: A delivery robot company measures battery life. Even if individual battery failures are unpredictable, the average battery life of a large fleet follows a predictable bell curve, allowing the company to guarantee delivery times.
